learnerMaterial.title: What a Decimal Expansion Reveals
learnerMaterial.subject: mathematics
learnerMaterial.lessonGoal: Today you will use decimal expansions to distinguish rational numbers from irrational numbers and justify an estimate.
successCriteria: I can identify terminating or repeating decimals as rational.
I can explain why a nonterminating, nonrepeating decimal is irrational.
I can bound an irrational number between decimals.
keyPoints: Every rational number has a decimal that terminates or repeats.
An irrational decimal continues without a repeating block.

vocabulary.definition: a decimal with finitely many nonzero digits
a decimal whose digit block repeats forever
a real number that cannot be written as a ratio of integers

sections.title: Worked example: bound √10
sections.directions: Read the completed reasoning. This is not a response page.

steps: The bounds are justified by squaring positive endpoints.

items.prompt: Which decimal form proves that 7/12 is rational?
choices: A decimal form cannot show this

feedback.correct: You recognized an eventually repeating block, which is a rational pattern.
feedback.incorrect: A rational decimal may terminate or begin with nonrepeating digits before a block repeats forever.

items.prompt: Classify 0.121212… as rational or irrational. Use the decimal pattern as evidence.

feedback.correct: You identified the repeating block and connected it to the rational-number rule.
feedback.incorrect: Mark a short block of digits and check whether that exact block repeats without end.

items.prompt: Enter the whole number immediately below √27.

feedback.correct: You used neighboring perfect squares to locate √27.
feedback.incorrect: Find consecutive perfect squares with 27 between them. Use the smaller square's root.

sections.title: Reteach: separate “goes on” from “does not repeat”
sections.body: A decimal going on forever is not enough to make it irrational. Repeating decimals also go on forever. Ask whether a fixed block repeats.

items.prompt: Which decimal description must be irrational?
choices: It continues forever with no repeating block.

feedback.correct: You used both conditions: nonterminating and nonrepeating.
feedback.incorrect: Eliminate patterns that rational numbers can have: terminating and repeating.

items.prompt: Explain why √15 is irrational, then place it between two consecutive tenths using squared endpoints.

feedback.correct: You combined the non-perfect-square argument with verified decimal bounds.
feedback.incorrect: First compare 15 with nearby perfect squares. Then test tenths by squaring positive endpoints.

whatYouLearned: Terminating and repeating decimals are rational.
Squared decimal endpoints can justify a square-root estimate.
